lesson.title: When Elements Combine: The Chemistry of Compounds
lesson.summary: This section explains how compounds form when elements bond in fixed ratios, and why a compound's properties can differ completely from its component elements.
lesson.body:
Elements rarely exist alone in nature. Far more often, atoms of different elements bond together to form compounds: pure substances made of two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed, whole number ratio. That fixed ratio is the key feature that separates a compound from a casual jumble of atoms. Water is always H2O, meaning every water molecule contains exactly two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, never three hydrogens or one and a half oxygens. This regularity is known as the law of definite proportions: any pure sample of a given compound always contains the same elements combined in the same mass ratio, no matter where the sample came from or how it was made. A sample of table salt from a mine in Poland and a sample evaporated from seawater in California are both NaCl, sodium bonded to chlorine in a one to one atomic ratio, and both are 39.3 percent sodium and 60.7 percent chlorine by mass.

What makes compounds especially interesting, and sometimes counterintuitive, is that their properties can be completely unlike the properties of the elements that formed them. Sodium is a soft, silvery metal so reactive that it must be stored under oil to keep it from reacting violently with moisture in the air. Chlorine is a pale yellow green gas that is toxic to breathe. Combine them chemically, however, and the product is sodium chloride, ordinary table salt: a white crystalline solid that is stable, nontoxic, and essential to your diet. Nothing about salt looks or behaves like either sodium metal or chlorine gas, because forming the compound involves a genuine chemical bond, in this case an ionic bond, that rearranges how the electrons are held and creates a new substance with its own distinct set of properties.

Chemical formulas are the shorthand chemists use to record exactly which elements a compound contains and in what ratio. In H2O, the subscript 2 tells you there are two hydrogen atoms for every one oxygen atom, oxygen's absence of a subscript means exactly one. In carbon dioxide, CO2, one carbon atom bonds with two oxygen atoms. In glucose, C6H12O6, the ratio is six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogen atoms, and six oxygen atoms, all bonded together into one molecule. These formulas are not arbitrary labels; they follow directly from how many bonds each element's atoms tend to form, a pattern rooted in the electron structure covered in the atoms section and refined further once you study bonding in later units.

Because compounds are held together by genuine chemical bonds, breaking a compound back into its component elements requires a chemical reaction, not just a physical process like heating, filtering, or stirring. Water can be split into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas through electrolysis, passing an electric current through it, but you cannot separate water into hydrogen and oxygen simply by boiling it; boiling only changes water's physical state, not its chemical identity. This distinction, between a compound's fixed composition held by chemical bonds and a mixture's variable composition with no bonding between components, is exactly the line the next section draws, when compounds are contrasted with mixtures.
